newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G20 banks move toward global foreign exchange bank.
newsitem.headline: G20 banks move toward global foreign exchange bank.

text.p: The creation of a new global bank to settle $1.2 trillion in daily foreign exchange transactions has moved closer as some of the world's major banks plan to set up a London-based company.

The company would be charged with developing a clearing and settlement bank and could include as shareholders a wide number of international banks and possibly institutions that net and settle foreign exchange transactions, such as London's Exchange Clearing House (ECHO) and U.S.-based Multinet International.
"We have moved from a loosely structured group of banks to shareholders of a company with a common mission," Stephen Thieke, managing director of J.P. Morgan, told Reuters in an interview.

Thieke is also chairman of the Group of 20 (G20), a group of major international banks that have proposed a global clearing house with the aim of drastically reducing the risk of breakdown in the foreign exchange settlement system, the backbone of the global financial system.

Payment and settlement systems are essential to the smooth functioning of financial markets and economies and the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations worry that many of the current systems expose banks to substantial interbank risks.

The nightmare that haunts central bankers is that the failure of one bank could lead to the failure of other banks due to these interbank exposures, triggering systemic risk to the worldwide financial system.
The decision to form the development company could be taken already this month and it would start operating immediately.

"We recognise that to put it into implementation we need the organisational stucture and the discipline of governance process and this will give us an opportunity reach out an include more than the initial G20," he said.

G20 Members include senior bankers from ABN Amro, Banque Nationale de Paris, Citibank, Credit Suisse, Deutsche BANK, Fuji Bank, HSBC Holdings, Royal Bank of Canada, Swiss Bank Corp, Societe Generale and Union Bank of Switzerland.

The development company would flush out the details for forming an actual bank, that is based on the principle of Continuous Linked Settlements (CLS) and bridges and connects national payment systems.

Thieke said a wide number of commercial banks and investment banks would be given the opportunity to become owners of the company, including the Group of 40, a grouping of 48 major commercial and investment banks from about 20 countries.

Thieke said G20 was still very interested in working closely together with the companies that provide netting services to "offer the financial industry an integrated solution that both has netting and fully CLS capabilities."
"We are keenly interested in pursuing this kind of participation," Thieke said about the participation of netting service providers.

The company could eventually develop into a holding company, opening up the possibility that the companies providing netting services could become part of an overall group that provides a one-stop shop for netting, clearing and settlement services.
"It provides us with some flexibility in case the opportunities to come closer together with the netting service providers presents themselves," Thieke said.
He declined to comment on the share capital of the company, which essentially would equal the estimated cost of developing a CLS bank.

Thieke stressed that the decision to locate the company was not a precursor of where a CLS bank would be based and the group was currently clarifying the legal and regulatory questions connected with setting up a bank.
"The decision where to locate the company and to develop the capability does not prejudge a decision about where you would locate a bank to provide services," he said.
Deciding where to located such a bank would also depend on how its services could be realigned with the netting companies.
